note: Enumerates 139 commonsense benchmarks and their flaws, which helps an audit judge whether a chosen test was fit for purpose.
title: Benchmarks for Automated Commonsense Reasoning: A Survey

reading.body:
Common sense testing for AI is not yet dependable: a survey of 139 benchmarks finds many are flawed and important abilities go untested.

The catalog splits by format. Of the 139 benchmarks, 102 use text, 18 use images, 12 use video, and 7 use simulated physical settings. The author examines twelve in detail, three per format, and surveys how these tests are built. The distribution matters because common sense in the physical world is the thinnest category, with only seven simulated environments, while the overwhelming majority of measurement happens in text.

The practical consequence is that a score on a common sense benchmark may not demonstrate the ability it names. If a vendor cites such a result, the useful questions are which test was used, whether it fits the intended use case, and how its quality was checked. The paper's recommendation is aimed at test makers: spend more effort so examples remain strong and uniform.

What the data does not cover is equally important. It reports no compute, energy, or facility figures, so it says nothing about what these benchmarks cost to run or where they run. It also gives no timeline beyond the 2023 publication year and no comparison of results across systems. The 94 citations indicate the survey is used, but the data here cannot show whether benchmark quality has improved since.

explain_beginner: This paper looks at tests used to check whether artificial intelligence systems understand everyday common sense. It lists 139 such tests: 102 use text, 18 use images, 12 use video, and 7 use simulated physical settings. The author describes twelve in more detail and reviews how these tests are built. The main finding is that many tests have problems, and important parts of common sense are not covered. So we cannot yet tell reliably how well AI systems handle common sense. This matters because people need trustworthy ways to judge how well AI systems handle these abilities, and the paper offers guidance for making future tests better.
explain_business: For leaders considering AI tools, this paper warns that common sense testing is not yet dependable. The author catalogs 139 tests, covering text, images, video, and simulated physical settings, and finds that many have flaws while other areas remain untested. That means a vendor's score on a common sense test may not prove the system has the ability being tested. The practical decision is to ask which test was used, whether it fits your use case, and how its quality was checked. The paper also advises test makers to spend effort so examples remain strong and uniform, which supports demanding better evidence before deployment.
explain_practitioner: The paper reviews the landscape of tests for machine common sense. It catalogs 139 benchmarks across four formats: 102 text, 18 image, 12 video, and 7 simulated physical. It then examines twelve examples, three per format, and surveys how such tests are constructed. It also discusses what common sense is, why AI needs it, what benchmark goals and desirable traits are, and where current tests fail or leave gaps. The key result is that existing coverage is incomplete and quality is uneven, so measurement is unreliable. The author recommends that test makers spend more effort so examples stay strong and uniform.
